title: Rental replacement by-law and Clair Road housing proposal
subtitle: Ward heritage district plan, Midtown Village design plan, growth monitoring report and two heritage designation notices.
overview: Council approved a rental replacement by-law, an enabling Official Plan amendment and a demolition control by-law amendment {{vote:m5}}. The tools let the City require that affordable rental units lost to demolition or conversion are replaced, starting with buildings of six or more units.

Council also held a statutory public meeting on a proposed high-density residential development at Clair Road West and Southgate Drive, and received the application {{vote:m6}}. No decision was made. Many delegates spoke, most in favour of the affordable home ownership model, others raising concerns about employment land, wildlife corridor changes and noise. Staff expect to report back in September.

Council received the draft Ward Heritage Conservation District plan {{vote:m7}} and the 2025 growth monitoring report {{vote:m8}}. It supported the Midtown Village concept plan at 64 Duke Street {{vote:m9}}. Notices of intention to designate two properties under the Ontario Heritage Act went ahead through the consent agenda.
After a closed session, the mayor reported that council gave direction to staff on an Ontario Land Tribunal matter and on a potential land acquisition. No further detail was given.

decisions.detail: Council approved the Rental Replacement By-law, the enabling Official Plan amendment and a demolition control by-law amendment, and found no further public notice was needed.

decisions.item: Clair Road West and Southgate Drive application
decisions.detail: Council received the statutory public meeting report on a proposed Official Plan and zoning amendment to allow high-density residential use; the application remains under staff review.
Council supported the urban design master plan concept plan, which is required before a formal development application can be submitted.
Council received the draft district plan and guidelines, with a final plan and recommendation expected in September.
Council received the 2025 report on progress toward Official Plan and provincial growth and housing targets.
The City Clerk was authorized to publish notice of intention to designate the property under the Ontario Heritage Act, with the by-law returning if no objections are received.

debate: Supporters of the Clair Road proposal, including employers, workers and community groups, said affordable home ownership near jobs would reduce long commutes and help employers keep staff. One councillor asked about safeguards against a bait-and-switch, and the applicant said it was open to a legally enforceable commitment.

Opponents and staff flagged concerns about converting employment land, relocating and narrowing the ecological linkage, noise near industry, and the City's possible liability for stormwater facilities in the linkage. Councillors asked staff to report on these and on endangered species protection.

On the Ward heritage plan, councillors and a delegate asked about enforcement and about allowing visible accessory dwelling units. Staff said they were considering more exemptions and that the plan could still prevent demolition of significant buildings. One councillor objected to regulating backyard units.

On Midtown Village, a delegate said building heights had risen since earlier consultation, parkland fell short of requirements, and affordability and non-residential uses were limited. The developer said tall buildings sit at the site centre with low-rise edges, and staff said parkland and traffic details would be reviewed in later applications.

On the growth report, councillors noted that housing starts depend on private builders, and that provincial funding tied to starts is hard for the City to control. Staff said financial pressure from lower development charges is expected to continue.
